description_full: Arista Networks, Inc. engages in the development, marketing, and sale of data-driven, client to cloud networking solutions for AI, data center, campus, and routing environments in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. Its cloud networking solutions consist of Extensible Operating System (EOS), a publish-subscribe state-sharing networking operating system offered in combination with a set of network applications. The company offers data center, cloud and AI networking, cognitive adjacencies, and cognitive network software and services. It also provides post contract customer support services, such as technical support, hardware repair and replacement parts beyond standard warranty, bug fixes, patches, and upgrade services. The company serves a range of industries comprising internet companies, cloud service providers, financial services organizations, government agencies, media and entertainment, healthcare, oil and gas, education, manufacturing, industrial, and others. It markets and sells its products through distributors, system integrators, value-added resellers, and original equipment manufacturer partners, as well as through its direct sales force. Arista Networks, Inc. was formerly known as Arastra, Inc. and changed its name to Arista Networks, Inc. in October 2008. The company was incorporated in 2004 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: Arista Networks, Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $215.8B market cap on $9.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +27% over the past three years and +27% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 132% against a 12% cost of capital — a 120-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 64% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $4.3B in free cash flow — roughly 47 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 17% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 43% operating margin runs 36pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.83x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+20.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 61% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 56% and a beta of 1.43, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.13 vs 5y 1.67), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $997.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $101 (margin of safety -70%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $47.98 to $218 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 45.8 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 35.2 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 50.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 46% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 28 covering analysts target $248 on average, 45% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 132% clears the cost of capital of 11.8% by 120pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.58).
It runs a 64% gross margin and converts 47% of revenue into free cash flow, or 42% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.25x.
ROE of 28% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 13.7% of revenue on R&D and 4.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $10.7B (1% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 20.8, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 256 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 27.1% over 3 years, 31.2% over 5 years and 26.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 59% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 42.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02, a backlog worth 30% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 92%.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (1.3% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 17.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 73%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (91 sales, net $291.8M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.7% (0.7% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 0.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 5,115 employees, each generates about $1.8M of revenue, 4.7x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 28.2% a year.
That works out to $831K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $609K (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
